TBH
TEE-bee-AYCH (or spoken in full)
abbreviation (Gen-Z slang)
Text abbreviation of to be honest, a long-standing English hedge. The initialism appears in internet forums and chat by the 2000s. c. 2013–2015 it became a teen social-media ritual on Instagram and Facebook ("like for a tbh"), in which each friend who liked a post received a short public verdict on themselves from the poster. In 2017 an anonymous-compliment app named tbh topped the app charts and was bought by Facebook. Now a general softener in speech and text.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang tbh prefixes an honest opinion, often one the hearer may not like: "tbh I don’t think he’s good for you," or simply "tbh I’m tired." In the mid-2010s it was also a game: like a post and receive a public "tbh" rating from the poster. The Christian observation: honesty is a virtue Scripture commands, and Scripture also tells us what honesty is for. "Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour" (Zec 8:16) — and Paul adds the manner and the aim: "speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ" (Eph 4:15). Honest words are meant to build a brother up toward Christ, not to win the room. Proverbs honours the hard word: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Pro 27:6), and the rebuker "shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue" (Pro 28:23). Yet a sentence can be true and still cruel, and the old "tbh" posts often were — frankness as a licence for a public put-down. The honesty God wants starts further in: "thou desirest truth in the inward parts" (Psa 51:6), a person honest with God about himself before he is honest with anyone else. A father tells his son: be the friend who tells the truth when it costs him; say it to the person and not about him; and say it in a way that leaves him nearer to Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z text-speak (2000s chat; teen social-media ritual c. 2013–2015) for "to be honest" — a frankness Scripture commends when it is spoken in love to build a brother up toward Christ.

expand to see more

TBH, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2005–present; chat and social media) "To be honest"; introduces a frank opinion. "Tbh I liked the first one better."

c. 2013–2015: a social-media game, "like for a tbh," in which the poster gave each liker a short public opinion of them; also the name of a 2017 anonymous-compliment app.

Older relatives a grandparent will know: "to be honest with you," "frankly," "candidly."

Webster (1828), root word truth: “TRUTH, noun 1. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be. The truth of history constitutes its whole value. We rely on the truth of the scriptural prophecies. My mouth shall speak truth Proverbs 8:7. Sanctify them through thy truth; thy word is truth John 17:17. 2.”

Decode for parents: usually a softener; when it introduces a verdict on another person, ask whether it was said to them or about them.

Key Scripture

Zec 8:16 — "These are the things that ye shall do; Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates:"

Eph 4:15 — "But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:"

Pro 27:6 — "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful."

Pro 28:23 — "He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue."

Psa 51:6 — "Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom."

Modern Corruption

TBH prizes frankness, which Scripture also prizes, but detaches it from love and from self-examination, so that honesty can become a licence for a public put-down.

expand to see more

There is something right in a generation that wants people to be real. Scripture is full of hard, honest speech — Nathan before David, Paul withstanding Peter to the face — and it calls the friend who wounds faithfully better than the enemy who kisses (Pro 27:6). A teen who will tell his friend "tbh you’re drifting" may be doing him the greatest kindness of the year. Flattery is the commoner sin, and Proverbs promises that the honest rebuker ends with "more favour" than the flatterer (Pro 28:23).

The corruption is honesty cut loose from its purpose. The mid-2010s "tbh" posts often handed out public ratings — "tbh you’re kind of fake" — under cover of candour. Paul does not say merely "speak the truth"; he says "speaking the truth in love" and gives the goal, that we "grow up into him in all things" (Eph 4:15). Honest words aimed at Christ are medicine; honest words aimed at an audience are often cruelty in a clean shirt. And honesty begins at home: "thou desirest truth in the inward parts" (Psa 51:6). The friend who is honest about his own sin is the one whose honesty about yours can be trusted.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English treowth (faithfulness, truth) → "to be honest" as a hedge → tbh in 2000s chat → c. 2013–2015 "like for a tbh" → general softener.

expand to see more

Old English treowth — faithfulness, pledged loyalty, truth

Latin honestus — honourable; English honest, upright and truthful

2000s forums and chat: initialism tbh

c. 2013–2015 Instagram and Facebook: "like for a tbh" ratings; 2017 tbh app

Now a softener in speech and text, kin to ngl

Usage

""tbh I don’t think you should go to that party.""

"Speak the truth in love, aiming at Christ (Eph 4:15)."

"Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6) — say it to him, not about him."
